TRADE DRESS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Corp · the distinctive red-and-white striped packaging and rounded bottle shape

DESCRIPTION OF THE TRADE DRESS AND STATEMENTS ON FUNCTIONALITY AND DISTINCTIVENESS
Acme Corp identifies the trade dress at issue as the following features of a product, its packaging, or a business's décor: the distinctive red-and-white striped packaging and rounded bottle shape, used in connection with: bottled beverages.

Regarding functionality, Acme Corp's current position is: the packaging design is ornamental and not essential to the product's use

Regarding distinctiveness, Acme Corp's current position is: five years of continuous, exclusive use and substantial advertising expenditure

This description reflects Acme Corp's current understanding, recorded for informational purposes only. It is not a legal determination that the described features are non-functional, distinctive, or otherwise protectable as trade dress, and no court, the USPTO, or any other body has made any such determination based on this document.

STATUTORY BASIS: TRADE DRESS CLAIMS UNDER THE GENERAL LANHAM ACT FALSE-DESIGNATION-OF-ORIGIN PROVISION
Federal law does not contain a standalone statute captioned "trade dress." A claim that another person's product packaging, product design, or décor infringes protectable trade dress is instead brought under the same general federal unfair-competition provision, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A), that creates civil liability for use in commerce of "any word, term, name, symbol, or device, or any combination thereof" likely to cause confusion as to the origin, sponsorship, or approval of goods or services. That statutory text — the same general false-designation-of-origin provision already addressed in this tool's Trademark Infringement Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet and Trademark Registration Information Sheet documents for word marks and logos — does not itself use the words "trade dress," "packaging," "product design," or "décor," and it does not single out a product's overall appearance as an example of a protectable "symbol" or "device." Courts and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office have long read this general confusion-based language to extend to a product's or service's overall look and feel — this reading is a judicial and administrative gloss on the statutory text, developed through case law, not language Congress wrote into this specific provision. Confirming that Congress itself has since treated "trade dress" as a recognized category of claim arising under this same statutory chapter, a separate provision in this same section — 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(3), addressed in this document's companion clause on functionality — expressly uses the phrase "trade dress" when allocating the burden of proof in an infringement action, even though the general cause-of-action language quoted above does not contain that phrase.

THE FUNCTIONALITY DOCTRINE: A CATEGORICAL BAR TO TRADE DRESS PROTECTION
Even if a product's or service's overall appearance is otherwise distinctive, federal law bars trade dress protection for any feature that is "functional." The functionality doctrine operates as a categorical limit: a functional feature is not protectable as trade dress no matter how distinctive it has become, because trade dress law protects source-identifying appearance, not useful product features — those are instead the subject of patent law, which has its own, time-limited protections. The statute itself does not define "functional" or list the specific facts a court weighs in deciding functionality (for example, whether a feature is "essential to the use or purpose of the article" or "affects the cost or quality of the article" — a formulation widely attributed to the courts and discussed further in this clause's gap note); what the statute does provide, expressly using the phrase "trade dress," is a burden-of-proof rule: in a civil action for trade dress infringement brought under this chapter, where the trade dress at issue is not registered on the principal register, the party asserting trade dress protection bears the burden of proving that the matter it seeks to protect is not functional. This means that, for unregistered trade dress, the burden of proof on functionality is placed on the person claiming trade dress rights, not on the person accused of infringing them.

DISTINCTIVENESS REQUIREMENT: INHERENT DISTINCTIVENESS AND SECONDARY MEANING
Trade dress, like other trademarks, is protectable only if it is distinctive — capable of identifying and distinguishing the source of goods or services, rather than merely decorating or describing them. Federal trademark law recognizes two routes to distinctiveness: a mark or trade dress can be "inherently distinctive" (distinctive from the moment of first use, without any need to show that consumers have come to associate it with a particular source), or it can acquire distinctiveness over time through use — commonly called "secondary meaning." The general federal registration statute expressly recognizes the secondary-meaning route: except for marks expressly excluded on other statutory grounds, nothing in the statute prevents registration of a mark that "has become distinctive of the applicant's goods in commerce," and the statute allows proof of substantially exclusive and continuous use for the five years before the distinctiveness claim as prima facie evidence of that distinctiveness. It is widely reported in trade dress case law — most significantly, the Supreme Court's decision in Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Samara Brothers, Inc., 529 U.S. 205 (2000) — that this general distinctiveness framework applies differently to different categories of trade dress: product packaging can potentially qualify as inherently distinctive, while product design (the shape or configuration of the product itself) is widely reported to never be inherently distinctive and to require proof of secondary meaning in every case. This document reports that distinction here because it is a significant, non-obvious feature of trade dress law that differs from ordinary word-mark or logo analysis, but the underlying case law establishing it was not independently verified this session (see this clause's gap note), and it should not be treated as a verified quotation from that decision.

FEDERAL REGISTRATION OF TRADE DRESS IS AVAILABLE BUT NOT REQUIRED
Federal registration is available for trade dress, but it is not required in order to have protectable trade dress rights. Registration can be sought on the principal register — the primary federal trademark register, and the one associated with the additional statutory benefits (such as constructive nationwide notice and eligibility for incontestable status) described in this tool's Trademark Registration Information Sheet — if the trade dress is shown to be inherently distinctive or to have acquired secondary meaning. Separately, federal law also maintains a supplemental register for marks not yet eligible for the principal register. The statute governing that register expressly identifies "package" and "configuration of goods" among the categories of subject matter that may be registered there, alongside more familiar categories like trademarks, symbols, and words — confirming that packaging and product-configuration trade dress are subject matter Congress specifically contemplated for federal registration — but the same statutory sentence also requires that the matter sought to be registered, "as a whole," be "not functional" and be "capable of distinguishing the applicant's goods or services." Apart from any registration, common-law trade dress rights can also exist, based on actual use and distinctiveness in the marketplace, in the same way this tool's existing trademark documents describe common-law rights existing for word marks and logos independent of registration.

REMEDIES FOR TRADE DRESS INFRINGEMENT: CROSS-REFERENCE TO THE GENERAL LANHAM ACT REMEDIAL FRAMEWORK
A trade dress infringement claim under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a) draws on the same general federal remedial framework available for other claims under that statute. This tool's existing Trademark Infringement Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet document separately addresses, with its own verified statutory citations, the monetary remedies available for a Lanham Act violation (the defendant's profits, the plaintiff's damages, costs, discretionary enhancement of damages, and attorney's fees limited to "exceptional cases," plus a separate mandatory treble-damages rule for certain counterfeiting) and the availability of injunctive relief. The statute governing injunctive relief expressly extends that remedy to actions to prevent "a violation under subsection (a) ... of section 1125" — the same subsection under which trade dress claims are brought — confirming that trade dress claims fall within, not outside, that existing remedial framework, rather than requiring this document to restate a separate, trade-dress-specific set of remedies.

  — 15 U.S.C. § 1116(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, injunctive relief extends to violations under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a), the trade dress cause-of-action subsection (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1116)

CALIFORNIA LAW: GENERAL UNFAIR COMPETITION STATUTE, NOT A TRADE-DRESS-SPECIFIC DOCTRINE
California does not have a standalone statute captioned "trade dress" or specifically addressed to product packaging or product design. California's general unfair competition statute defines "unfair competition" broadly, to mean and include "any unlawful, unfair or fraudulent business act or practice" as well as unfair, deceptive, untrue, or misleading advertising and violations of the state's separate false-advertising statute. This definition is not limited to any specific subject matter, and it does not mention trademarks, trade dress, packaging, or product design; by its own terms, it could potentially reach conduct involving a product's or service's appearance to the same broad extent it could reach any other unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business conduct. Whether, and to what extent, this general statute has actually been applied by California courts to trade-dress-type claims specifically is a question this clause does not resolve; no case law confirming or describing such an application was verified this session (see this clause's gap note).

expectedJSON.body: Federal registration is available for trade dress, but it is not required in order to have protectable trade dress rights. Registration can be sought on the principal register — the primary federal trademark register, and the one associated with the additional statutory benefits (such as constructive nationwide notice and eligibility for incontestable status) described in this tool's Trademark Registration Information Sheet — if the trade dress is shown to be inherently distinctive or to have acquired secondary meaning. Separately, federal law also maintains a supplemental register for marks not yet eligible for the principal register. The statute governing that register expressly identifies "package" and "configuration of goods" among the categories of subject matter that may be registered there, alongside more familiar categories like trademarks, symbols, and words — confirming that packaging and product-configuration trade dress are subject matter Congress specifically contemplated for federal registration — but the same statutory sentence also requires that the matter sought to be registered, "as a whole," be "not functional" and be "capable of distinguishing the applicant's goods or services." Apart from any registration, common-law trade dress rights can also exist, based on actual use and distinctiveness in the marketplace, in the same way this tool's existing trademark documents describe common-law rights existing for word marks and logos independent of registration.

expectedJSON.body: California does not have a standalone statute captioned "trade dress" or specifically addressed to product packaging or product design. California's general unfair competition statute defines "unfair competition" broadly, to mean and include "any unlawful, unfair or fraudulent business act or practice" as well as unfair, deceptive, untrue, or misleading advertising and violations of the state's separate false-advertising statute. This definition is not limited to any specific subject matter, and it does not mention trademarks, trade dress, packaging, or product design; by its own terms, it could potentially reach conduct involving a product's or service's appearance to the same broad extent it could reach any other unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business conduct. Whether, and to what extent, this general statute has actually been applied by California courts to trade-dress-type claims specifically is a question this clause does not resolve; no case law confirming or describing such an application was verified this session (see this clause's gap note).
